def shipping_heavy_value(rows):
    """Quick favor before the three o'clock pallet run leaves the dock.

    You know how the warehouse export works by now: the manifest tool dumps
    every line item into a bare list of lists, no headers, no objects, just
    rows straight off the packing floor. Each element of rows is a list of
    exactly three values: a name (str), a qty (int), and a unit (int). The
    name is whatever the packing station typed on the label, qty is how many
    of that item sit on the manifest line, and unit is the declared
    per-item value.

    Here's why I'm pinging you. Our freight insurer sent over their
    quarterly paperwork this morning, and buried in it is a line asking for
    the total declared value of our bulk shipments — the big entries, the
    ones that actually matter when a pallet goes missing off a truck. The
    small stuff they don't want cluttering the figure; a lonely box of two
    staplers isn't what anyone files a claim over. I'd rather encode their
    cutoff once in a tiny helper than have three of us eyeballing
    spreadsheets every quarter and getting three different answers.

    So, plainly: Return the sum of qty * unit over the rows with qty
    greater than or equal to 20.

    That's the whole job. Ops will call this from the reporting script
    right after the export lands, so it just needs to take the rows and
    hand back one number the insurer can drop straight into their form. I
    already wired up the call site and the export itself; this helper is
    the only missing piece before we ship the report tonight. Once it's
    merged, the quarterly filing becomes a one-liner for whoever is on
    rotation that week, which future-us will very much appreciate. Couple
    of quick sanity checks below so you can see it behaving on an empty
    manifest and on a single line item.

    >>> shipping_heavy_value([])
    0
    >>> shipping_heavy_value([['error', 41, 3]])
    123
    """
